{{Short description|Important mathematical operations in quantum mechanics}}
{{Other uses|Transformation (disambiguation){{!}}Transformation}}
{{Use American English|date=January 2019}}

In [[quantum mechanics]], the [[Schrödinger equation]] describes how a system changes with time. It does this by relating changes in the state of the system to the energy in the system (given by an operator called the [[Hamiltonian (quantum mechanics)|Hamiltonian]]). Therefore, once the Hamiltonian is known, the time dynamics are in principle known. All that remains is to plug the Hamiltonian into the Schrödinger equation and solve for the system state as a function of time.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Sakurai |first1=J. J. |last2=Napolitano |first2=Jim J. |title=[[Modern Quantum Mechanics]] |date=2014 |publisher=Pearson |isbn=978-93-325-1900-8 |pages=67–72 |edition=Indian Subcontinent Version}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Griffiths |first1=David J. |title=Introduction to Quantum Mechanics |url=https://archive.org/details/introductiontoqu00grif_190 |url-access=limited |date=2005 |publisher=Pearson |isbn=978-0-13-191175-8 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/introductiontoqu00grif_190/page/n35 24]–29 |edition=Second}}</ref>

Often, however, the Schrödinger equation is difficult to solve ([[Numerical methods for ordinary differential equations|even with a computer]]). Therefore, physicists have developed mathematical techniques to simplify these problems and clarify what is happening physically. One such technique is to apply a '''unitary transformation''' to the Hamiltonian. Doing so can result in a simplified version of the Schrödinger equation which nonetheless has the same solution as the original.

== Transformation ==
A unitary transformation (or frame change) can be expressed in terms of a time-dependent Hamiltonian <math>H(t)</math> and unitary operator <math>U(t)</math>. Under this change, the Hamiltonian transforms as:

:<math>H \to UH{U^\dagger} + i\hbar\,{\dot{U}U^\dagger}
=: \breve{H} \quad \quad (0)</math>.

The Schrödinger equation applies to the new Hamiltonian. Solutions to the untransformed and transformed equations are also related by <math>U</math>. Specifically, if the [[wave function]] <math>\psi(t)</math> satisfies the original equation, then <math>U\psi(t)</math> will satisfy the new equation.<ref>{{cite thesis |last=Axline |first=Christopher J. |date=2018 |title=Building Blocks for Modular Circuit QED Quantum Computing |type=Ph.D. thesis |chapter=Chapter 6 |chapter-url=https://rsl.yale.edu/sites/default/files/files/Chris%20Axline%20-%20Thesis%20-%20smaller.pdf |access-date=4 August 2018}}</ref>

=== Derivation ===
Recall that by the definition of a [[unitary matrix]], <math>U^\dagger U = I</math>. Beginning with the Schrödinger equation,

:<math>\dot{\psi}=-\frac{i}{\hbar}H\psi</math>,

we can therefore insert the identity <math>U^\dagger U=I</math> at will. In particular, inserting it after <math>H/\hbar</math> and also premultiplying both sides by <math>U</math>, we get

:<math>U\dot{\psi}=-\frac{i}{\hbar} \left(UHU^\dagger \right) U\psi\quad\quad (1)</math>.

Next, note that by the [[product rule]],

:<math>\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(U\psi\right)=\dot{U}\psi+U\dot{\psi}</math>.

Inserting another <math>U^\dagger U</math> and rearranging, we get

:<math>U\dot{\psi} =
\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d t}\Big(U\psi\Big)
- \dot{U}U^\dagger U\psi \quad\quad(2)</math>.

Finally, combining (1) and (2) above results in the desired transformation:

:<math>\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d t}\Big(U \psi\Big) = 
-\frac{i}{\hbar}\Big(UH{U^\dagger} + i\hbar\, \dot{U}{U^\dagger}\Big)
\Big(U\psi\Big) \quad\quad \left(3\right)</math>.

If we adopt the notation <math>\breve{\psi} := U\psi</math> to describe the transformed wave function, the equations can be written in a clearer form. For instance, <math>(3)</math> can be rewritten as

:<math>\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d t}\breve{\psi} = 
-\frac{i}{\hbar} \breve{H}\breve{\psi}
\quad\quad \left(4\right)</math>,

which can be rewritten in the form of the original Schrödinger equation,

:<math>\breve{H}\breve{\psi} =
i\hbar{\operatorname{d}\!\breve{\psi}\over\operatorname{d}\!t}.</math>

The original wave function can be recovered as <math>\psi = U^{\dagger} \breve{\psi}</math>.

=== Relation to the interaction picture ===
Unitary transformations can be seen as a generalization of the [[Interaction picture|interaction (Dirac) picture]]. In the latter approach, a Hamiltonian is broken into a time-independent part and a time-dependent part,

:<math>H(t)=H_0 + V(t) \quad \quad (a)</math>.

In this case, the Schrödinger equation becomes

:<math>\dot{\psi_I} =
-\frac{i}{\hbar} \left(e^{iH_0 t/\hbar} V e^{-iH_0 t/\hbar}\right) \psi_I</math>, with <math>\psi_I = e^{i H_0 t/\hbar} \psi</math>.<ref name=":0">Sakurai, pp. 346-350.</ref>

The correspondence to a unitary transformation can be shown by choosing <math display="inline">U(t)=\exp\left[{+i H_0 t / \hbar}\right]</math>. As a result, <math>{U^\dagger}(t) = \exp \left[{-i H_{0} t}/\hbar\right].</math>

Using the notation from <math>(a)</math> above, our transformed Hamiltonian becomes

:<math>\breve{H} = U\left[H_0 + V(t)\right]U^{\dagger} + i\hbar \dot{U}U^{\dagger}
\quad \quad (b)</math>

First note that since <math>U</math> is a function of <math>H_0</math>, the two must [[Commutative property|commute]]. Then

:<math>UH_0U^\dagger=H_0</math>,

which takes care of the first term in the transformation in <math>(b)</math>, i.e. <math>\breve{H} = H_0 + UV(t)U^{\dagger} + i \hbar \dot{U}U^{\dagger}</math>. Next use the [[chain rule]] to calculate

:<math>\begin{align} i\hbar \dot{U}U^\dagger  & =
i\hbar \left({\operatorname{d}\!U\over\operatorname{d}\!t}\right) e^{-iH_{0} t/\hbar} \\
& = i\hbar \Big(iH_{0}/\hbar\Big) e^{+iH_{0} t/\hbar} e^{-iH_{0} t/\hbar} \\
& = i \hbar \left({i H_0}/\hbar \right) \\
& = -H_{0}, \\ \end{align}</math>

which cancels with the other <math>H_0</math>. Evidently we are left with <math>\breve{H} = UVU^\dagger</math>, yielding <math>\dot{\psi_{I}} = -\frac{i}{\hbar} U V U^{\dagger} \psi_I </math> as shown above.

When applying a general unitary transformation, however, it is not necessary that <math>H(t)</math> be broken into parts, or even that <math>U(t)</math> be a function of any part of the Hamiltonian.

== Examples ==

=== Rotating frame ===
Consider an atom [[Two-state quantum system|with two states]], [[Ground state|ground state]] <math>|g\rangle</math> and [[Excited state|excited state]] <math>|e\rangle</math>. The atom has a Hamiltonian <math>H = \hbar\omega {|{e}\rangle \langle {e}|}</math>, where <math>\omega</math> is the [[frequency]] of [[light]] associated with the ground-to-excited [[Atomic electron transition|transition]]. Now suppose we illuminate the atom with a [[Driven harmonic motion|drive]] at frequency <math>\omega_d</math> which [[Coupling (physics)|couples]] the two states, and that the time-dependent driven Hamiltonian is

:<math>H/\hbar=\omega |e\rangle\langle e| + \Omega\ e^{i\omega_d t}|g\rangle\langle e| + \Omega^*\ e^{-i\omega_d t}|e\rangle\langle g|</math>

for some complex drive strength <math>\Omega</math>. Because of the competing frequency scales (<math>\omega</math>, <math>\omega_d</math>, and <math>\Omega</math>), it is difficult to anticipate the effect of the drive (see [[driven harmonic motion]]).

Without a drive, the phase of <math>|e\rangle</math> would oscillate relative to <math>|g\rangle</math>. In the [[Bloch sphere]] representation of a two-state system, this corresponds to rotation around the z-axis. Conceptually, we can remove this component of the dynamics by entering a [[Rotating reference frame|rotating frame of reference]] defined by the unitary transformation <math>U=e^{i\omega t|e\rangle\langle e|}</math>. Under this transformation, the Hamiltonian becomes

:<math>H/\hbar\to \Omega\, e^{i(\omega_d-\omega)t} |g\rangle \langle e| 
+ \Omega^*\, e^{i(\omega-\omega_d)t} |e\rangle \langle g|</math>.

If the driving frequency is equal to the g-e transition's frequency, <math>\omega_d=\omega</math>, [[resonance]] will occur and then the equation above reduces to

:<math>\breve{H} / \hbar =
\Omega\ |g\rangle\langle e| + \Omega^*\ |e\rangle\langle g|</math>.

From this it is apparent, even without getting into details, that the dynamics will involve an [[oscillation]] between the ground and excited states at frequency <math>\Omega</math>.<ref name=":0" />

As another limiting case, suppose the drive is far off-resonant, <math>|\omega_d-\omega|\gg 0</math>. We can figure out the dynamics in that case without solving the Schrödinger equation directly. Suppose the system starts in the ground state <math>|g\rangle</math>. Initially, the Hamiltonian will populate some component of <math>|e\rangle</math>. A small time later, however, it will populate roughly the same amount of <math>|e\rangle</math> but with completely different phase. Thus the effect of an off-resonant drive will tend to cancel itself out. This can also be expressed by saying that an off-resonant drive is [[Rotating wave approximation|''rapidly rotating'' in the frame of the atom]].

=== Displaced frame ===
The example above could also have been analyzed in the interaction picture. The following example, however, is more difficult to analyze without the general formulation of unitary transformations. Consider two [[Quantum harmonic oscillator|harmonic oscillators]], between which we would like to engineer a [[beam splitter]] interaction,

:<math>g\, ab^\dagger + g^*\, a^\dagger b</math>.

This was achieved experimentally with two [[microwave cavity]] resonators serving as <math>a</math> and <math>b</math>.<ref>{{Cite journal |author=Yvonne Y. Gao |author2= Brian J. Lester|display-authors=etal|date=21 June 2018|title=Programmable Interference between Two Microwave Quantum Memories|journal=Phys. Rev. X|volume=8|issue=2|at=Supplemental Material|arxiv=1802.08510|doi=10.1103/PhysRevX.8.021073|s2cid= 3723797}}</ref> Below, we sketch the analysis of a simplified version of this experiment.

In addition to the microwave cavities, the experiment also involved a [[transmon]] [[qubit]], <math>c</math>, coupled to both modes. The qubit is driven simultaneously at two frequencies, <math>\omega_1</math> and <math>\omega_2</math>, for which <math>\omega_1-\omega_2=\omega_a-\omega_b</math>.

:<math>H_\mathrm{drive}/\hbar=\Re\left[\epsilon_1e^{i\omega_1 t}+\epsilon_2 e^{i\omega_2 t}\right](c+c^\dagger).</math>

In addition, there are many [[Orders of approximation#Higher-order|fourth-order]] terms [[Mode coupling|coupling the modes]], but most of them can be neglected. In this experiment, two such terms which will become important are

:<math>H_4/\hbar=g_4\Big(e^{i(\omega_b-\omega_a)t}ab^\dagger + \text{h.c.}\Big)c^\dagger c</math>.

(H.c. is [[Abuse of notation|shorthand]] for the [[Hermitian conjugate]].) We can apply a [[Displacement operator|displacement]] transformation, <math>U=D(-\xi_1 e^{-i\omega_1 t}-\xi_2 e^{-i\omega_2 t})</math>, to mode <math>c</math>{{Clarify|reason=what is the transformation used for?|date=September 2018}}. For carefully chosen amplitudes, this transformation will cancel <math>H_\textrm{drive}</math> while also displacing the [[ladder operator]], <math>c\to c+\xi_1 e^{-i\omega_1 t}+\xi_2 e^{-i\omega_2 t}</math>. This leaves us with

:<math>H/\hbar = g_4\Big(e^{i(\omega_b-\omega_a)t}ab^\dagger + e^{i(\omega_a-\omega_b)t}a^\dagger b\big)(c^\dagger +\xi_1^* e^{i\omega_1t}+\xi_2^* e^{i\omega_2 t})(c +\xi_1 e^{-i\omega_1t}+\xi_2 e^{-i\omega_2 t})</math>.

Expanding this expression and dropping the rapidly rotating terms, we are left with the desired Hamiltonian,

:<math>H/\hbar=g_4 \xi_1^*\xi_2 e^{i(\omega_b-\omega_a+\omega_1-\omega_2)t}\ ab^\dagger+\text{h.c.} = g\, ab^\dagger + g^*\, a^\dagger b</math>.

=== Relation to the [[Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff formula]] ===
It is common for the operators involved in unitary transformations to be written as exponentials of operators, <math>U = e^X</math>, as seen above. Further, the operators in the exponentials commonly obey the relation <math>X^\dagger = -X</math>, so that the transform of an operator <math>Y</math> is,<math>UYU^\dagger = e^XYe^{-X}</math>. By now introducing the iterator commutator,

: <math>[(X)^n,Y] \equiv \underbrace{[X,\dotsb[X,[X}_{n \text { times }}, Y]] \dotsb],\quad [(X)^0,Y] \equiv Y,</math>

we can use a special result of the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff formula to write this transformation compactly as,

: <math>e^X Y e^{-X} = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{[(X)^n,Y]}{n!},</math>

or, in long form for completeness,

: <math>e^{X}Y e^{-X} = Y+\left[X,Y\right]+\frac{1}{2!}[X,[X,Y]]+\frac{1}{3!}[X,[X,[X,Y]]]+\cdots.</math>
